result.keywords: This study compares multiple sampling schemes for event-based landslide susceptibility mapping using recurrent neural networks, focusing on how inventory construction and class balance affect predictive stability. The experiment examines source and run-out landslide representations, evaluates hybrid and spatially stratified sampling, and tests cost-sensitive training to reduce false alarms and omission errors. A typhoon-triggered landslide dataset from southern Taiwan is used to assess model robustness under different preprocessing settings. Results indicate that separating run-out areas as an independent class improves classification consistency, while balanced sampling generally yields higher overall accuracy and kappa than naive random sampling. The paper highlights the importance of aligning sampling design with geomorphic heterogeneity when building data-driven susceptibility models.
result.title: Comparative Analysis of Sampling Schemes for Event-Based Landslide Susceptibility Mapping with Recurrent Neural Networks
